column1: # design decision D2: "keep the shell literals, lint them for equality" — a
# TSV of every existing setting, populated with defaults matching the shell
# literals EXACTLY, so a future equality lint (a LATER item,
# registry-config-lints) starts green with no baseline needed. This file is
# header for the parse/union contract and the overlay extension format.
# name           the shell variable name (exact, case-sensitive).
# default        the CURRENT shell literal, copied verbatim from the
#                interpolation written as-is (never pre-resolved). A blank
#                field means the literal default IS the empty string.
# type           closed set (see below) — the KIND of value, not its
# layer          closed set (see below) — which layer of the six-layer config
#                DEFAULT lives at. Almost every row is `kernel` (an
#                individual script's own hardcoded layer-6 fallback) or
#                that file IS the committed config a consuming repo vendors
#                and edits, per its own header). A var whose default
#                genuinely DIFFERS between two owning scripts (a real layer-5
#                vs layer-6 divergence, not just a byte-identical duplicate
#                fallback — see below) gets TWO rows, one per layer.
# owning-script  repo-relative path to the script whose `:=`/`:-` line this
#                row transcribes. Several settings have a BYTE-IDENTICAL `:=`
#                fallback duplicated in more than one consuming script
#                (documented in each duplicate site's own comment as
#                also has a matching literal in pipeline-drive.sh and
#                pipeline-tick.sh); this registry records ONE row citing the
#                script documented as the SOURCE OF TRUTH (build.config.sh
#                where one exists) rather than one row per duplicate site,
#                since the literals are identical and a future equality
#                lint gains nothing from redundant rows.
#                  A SECOND, differently-shaped duplicate exists and follows
#                the same one-row rule for a different reason: a CONSUMING
#                CALLER that PINS a registered setting to a value the owning
#                script cannot know, before invoking that owner. The live case
#                emit-model-usage.sh, correctly defaults to a checkout-relative
#                path and deliberately refuses to guess a foreign one, so its
#                spawn.sh) each export the canonical absolute sink themselves.
#                Those literals DIFFER from the owner's on purpose, so — unlike
#                the byte-identical case above — a second row would be WRONG
#                twice over: it would assert a default the owner does not have,
#                and the equality check walks EVERY seam for a name in a row's
#                owning-script, so the callers' own `${NAME:-}` set-ness guard
#                would fail it. One row, owner's literal, and each caller
#                documents its pin in its own comment. The unregistered sweep is
#                name-only by design, which is what keeps a caller pin legal.
# doc            one-line description of what the setting controls.
#   string   free-form text with no narrower type below
#   enum     a closed set of string values (see the doc column for the set)
#   path     a filesystem path, or a bare binary name resolved via PATH
#   label    a GitHub label / branch / literal identifier string
#   marker   an HTML-comment idempotency marker embedded in issue/PR bodies
# The six-layer ladder's own tokens (docs/config-precedence.md). Layers 1-2
# (cli, env) never appear here — a registry row records a DEFAULT, and layers
# 1-2 are call-site/environment inputs, never a hardcoded default:
#   cli            layer 1 — CLI flag (never a registry row; listed for
#   env            layer 2 — env var (never a registry row; ditto)
#   machine-conf   layer 3 — a machine-wide conf file
#   repo-local     layer 4 — an untracked, gitignored repo-local conf file
#   tracked-repo   layer 5 — a COMMITTED config file's own `:=` default
#                  (build.config.sh today — the file IS the tracked conf)
#   kernel         layer 6 — a hardcoded `:=`/`:-` fallback in an individual
#                  script, for a non-vendoring caller that never sources a
# A row exists for every `${VAR:-default}` / `: "${VAR:=default}"` shell
# seam an OPERATOR could meaningfully override via the config precedence
# ladder to change behavior. Excluded: internal/derived/computed values
# (timestamps, loop counters, computed paths built from other already-
# environment-detection predicates (`${TMUX:-}` — "am I inside tmux?", not a
# OS/XDG passthrough vars with no project-specific override point of their
# explicitly documented as such in their own script (`BUILD_QUOTA_NOW`,
# `PIPELINE_NOW_*`). A "test-double seam for the <X> binary" row (e.g.
# `*_GH_BIN`) IS included — swapping the resolved binary is a real,
# meaningful override, not merely a test's implementation detail.
# ── Renamed env-var rows (temperloop#165, the foundation→temperloop rename) ──
# TEMPERLOOP_VERSION were renamed from FOUNDATION_* in v0.15.0. Through the
# read-old window each new row's default transcribed a nested
# `${FOUNDATION_*:-...}` fallback and a DEPRECATED legacy row sat beside it.
# Both are GONE as of v0.19.0: the four legacy rows were REMOVED (a removed
# row-name, i.e. BREAKING per the rule above, carried by the v0.15.0
# CHANGELOG BREAKING entry's stated window) and each surviving row's default
# is now the bare built-in value its owning script actually reads. The legacy
# NAMES still appear in those scripts — but only inside a detect-and-refuse
# arm, which is not a read and so is not a registry setting; see
# Two rows below (TEMPERLOOP_KERNEL_REPO and KERNEL_REMOTE) record a CURRENT
# default that is this org's real repo clone URL — permanent, load-bearing,
# out of scrub scope (this repo's own public identity, not a personal-token
# leak; see check-personal-token-denylist.sh's category-1 rationale). They
# carry an explicit `denylist:allow` marker substring in their doc column
# check-personal-token-denylist.sh's marker-skip already uses in shell
# files, adapted to TSV's data-not-code rows, since the checker's marker
# test is a bare substring match, not shell-comment syntax) — those rows
# would otherwise register as NEW denylist hits, and the burn-down baseline
# mechanism explicitly does not accept new rows for an already-tracked
# family (see personal-token-denylist-baseline.tsv's own header). These are
# permanent, documented, load-bearing defaults, not scrub debt — exactly the
# A THIRD row used to live here — KNOWLEDGE_STORE_ROOT's build.config.sh
# reseed to the operator's personal vault directory. kernel-literal-scrub
# removed that reseed (build.config.sh no longer sets a layer-5 default for
# this setting at all) rather than allow-marking it, so the row was deleted
# rather than converted — see the kernel-layer KNOWLEDGE_STORE_ROOT row
# (owning-script knowledge_store.sh) below for the setting's one remaining
# TEMPERLOOP_PROFILE (below) is a RESERVED row, not a live seam today: no
# script reads it yet. The profile mechanism itself (named config profiles
# an operator switches between) is deferred (Bucket C of the D2 design); this
# row only reserves the name + default so a future implementation has an
# uncontested slot and the registry's shape doesn't change out from under
# an equality lint when that lands.

Wall-clock LIVENESS ceiling, in seconds, on assess.md Step 3's whole review-subagent fanout (requirements-auditor, plus the conditional architecture-reviewer), measured from the moment the reviewers are spawned. Step 3 had NO time or cost bound: its graceful skip covers an UNAVAILABLE agent, never a NON-TERMINATING one, so a reviewer that was resolved, spawned and is still actively working is invisible to that probe. temperloop#866 (/assess --epic 856): architecture-reviewer returned in 336s over 20 tool uses while requirements-auditor ran more than three hours and 235KB of transcript on comparable scope before the operator killed it by hand -- not hung, just working, at ~32x its sibling's cost for a bounded read-only review. On an unattended run nobody interrupts it and /assess never reaches Step 4 to write the plan note at all. Reviewers now spawn CONCURRENTLY in the background and the fanout waits under this one ceiling in backgrounded sleep slices; a reviewer still unreturned at it is ABANDONED (the bound is on the WAIT, not on the agent) and Step 3 continues to Step 3.5 with whatever DID return, emitting the `skipped -- <agent> timed out after <actual>s` degradation notice (claude/message-schema.md section Degradation notice, ceiling-timeout shape) so an incomplete review never reads as a clean one. DELIBERATELY NOT a reuse of BUILD_REVIEW_AGENT_CEILING_SECS: that pair rides the build-level.mjs input.reviewAgentCeilingSecs seam /assess never touches, its breach arm can escalate review-agent-timeout and refuse to push (every Step-3 reviewer is advisory, so there is no such arm here), and it bounds one item's diff review rather than a whole epic's draft decomposition. Resolved at assess.md Step 0 item 6; belt-and-suspenders ${ASSESS_REVIEW_AGENT_CEILING_SECS:-900} on a checkout that does not vendor this config file

Observability half of ASSESS_REVIEW_AGENT_CEILING_SECS: an assess.md Step-3 review fanout still outstanding after this many seconds emits a one-line progress notice naming which reviewers are still running, so a long-but-alive review is visible well before the ceiling gives up on it instead of the silence temperloop#866 was. A slow reviewer is NOT abandoned and NOT dispositioned. It also sets the bounded wait's FIRST slice, so a review finishing inside this threshold costs exactly one backgrounded sleep. Seeded above the incident's observed healthy review (336s) so a healthy run stays quiet. 0 disables the notice. Kept below the ceiling, where it could never fire. Resolved at assess.md Step 0 item 6

NO subtraction pass ran, and that is the deliberate call rather than an omission: build.md's per-outcome disposition list is precisely the mechanism that stops an undocumented payload shape from becoming a silent stall, so folding this bullet into the neighbouring PUSH_REJECTED one would misfile a distinct outcome, and trimming an unrelated contract line to buy the line back would delete more contract surface than the one-line ratchet step costs. Convergence bound on claude/workflows/build-level.mjs's §3e pre-push review loop: the number of review ROUNDS one item's worktree may spend before a HIGH-severity finding stops escalating `review-blocking` (which loops the item back to 3c for another worker+review round) and is instead carried into the PR body's `## Review notes` plus the parked record's review.residual_blocking tally for the human at the merge gate. Largest PR body, in BYTES, that workflows/scripts/build/pr.sh will hand to `gh pr create` / `gh pr edit`. GitHub rejects a body over 65536 characters (`GraphQL: Body is too long`), and that rejection lands on the LAST step of PR-open -- after the worker, every routed reviewer, the acceptance gate, the activation gate and the push have already succeeded, so the branch is safe but the result cannot be published and an unattended run parks a finished item (two live occurrences in one day: temperloop#1958, #1970, both recovered by hand). Past this bound pr.sh truncates LOCALLY instead: verbatim reviewer prose first, oldest review round first (a ROUND, not one reviewer's block -- a round that routed three reviewers renders three blocks and they go together), then the newest round's prose tail with every reviewer name and finding heading in it kept, then the middle of the verification surface -- each cut leaving an inline marker naming what went, how much, and where the full text can be read. Never cut at any rung: the bare `Closes #N` linkage lines, the acceptance recap, the `## Verification` heading, the backlinks or the attribution footer. Bytes rather than characters is conservative in the safe direction (a UTF-8 byte count is >= the character count GitHub meters); 60000 leaves headroom below 65536 for that linkage + attribution tail. A non-numeric or zero value falls back to pr.sh's own in-file default rather than disabling the bound. Read by pr.sh directly (it sources build.config.sh), which is also where its byte-identical non-vendoring-checkout fallback lives

Whether claude/workflows/build-level.mjs's 3e.5 parent-side acceptance gate runs DIFF-SCOPED (1, the default: only the gates the item's changed paths reach, resolved through workflows/scripts/config/gate-paths.tsv) or as the full repo-wide suite (0, the pre-temperloop#1663 behavior). A full per-item suite could not survive within-level parallelism -- a measured 3-item level spent 55 min and 1.24M subagent tokens and landed ZERO items, all three escalating acceptance-gate-timeout with every worker already finished and committed -- and the budget cannot absorb it, since GATE_SLICE_SECS_MAX sits only ~20% above the budget that failed and is clamped by the executor agent's own ~10-min Bash cap. Scoping puts 3e.5 on the same footing as the pull_request run of CI's checks job, which has used this same map since temperloop#1024; what gates `main` is unchanged, because the merge_group run is unscoped. Read in the EMITTED SHELL from the worktree's own copy of build.config.sh rather than plumbed as an orchestrator input.* key like BUILD_GATE_SLICE_SECS (which must reach the .mjs's own control flow); the #1241 env scrub leaves the machine-conf and repo-local config FILE layers intact, so those remain the escape hatch

Per-STEP wall-clock liveness bound, in seconds, on a claude/workflows/build-level.mjs machinery-executor step (prelude/pr-batch/ci-batch batches and the solo gate/recover-probe/push-retry calls). Enforced INSIDE the emitted shell (a bash+sleep+kill watchdog modelled on workflows/scripts/lib/portable-timeout.sh's dependency-free fallback tier), independently of and in addition to the Bash tool's own `timeout` parameter — because temperloop#1071 observed a pr-batch step run 9h49m with the tool timeout never firing and nothing else bounding the call. A step that outlives the ceiling is killed, reports {"outcome":"STEP_TIMEOUT"}, and is treated as LOST: the driver runs the existing pr.sh recover-probe side-effect ladder (temperloop#939) and ADOPTS an already-opened PR rather than re-issuing anything, so a bounded step can never double-push or double-open. Resolved at build.md/sweep.md/fix.md Step 0 and passed as the orchestrator-supplied workflow input input.machineryStepCeilingSecs (the Workflow runtime has no shell to source build.config.sh itself, and no Date.now() to measure with — DESIGN NOTE 1); the .mjs keeps its own in-file default and enforces a floor so no value can bound a step below one CI poll slice

Observability half of BUILD_MACHINERY_STEP_CEILING_SECS: a BATCHED build-level.mjs machinery step that takes at least this many seconds emits an extra {"outcome":"STEP_SLOW"} notice line alongside its real result, which the driver partitions out of the results array and turns into a log() line — so a long stall is visible long before it reaches the ceiling, instead of being the silent 9h49m of temperloop#1071. A slow step is NOT lost and is NOT disposed. 0 disables the notice. Deliberately NOT applied to the SOLO executor calls, whose schema admits exactly one JSON object. Resolved at build.md/sweep.md/fix.md Step 0 and passed as input.machineryStepSlowSecs

Wall-clock LIVENESS ceiling, in seconds, on claude/workflows/build-level.mjs's whole §3e pre-push review fanout, measured from the moment the routed reviewers are spawned. The sibling of BUILD_MACHINERY_STEP_CEILING_SECS one layer up: that one bounds a machinery STEP via a watchdog compiled into the emitted shell, but a §3e reviewer is an agent({agentType}) call with no shell to wrap, so it had no bound at all. temperloop#2003 (run wf_f3b9c160-6ca): one reviewer was spawned and never returned, the workflow stopped writing its journal for ~41 minutes, and the MANDATORY workflow-reviewer for that item's claude/commands/*.md diff never launched -- so review.mandatory_ok was never even evaluated. Reviewers now run CONCURRENTLY and the fanout waits under this one ceiling; a reviewer still unreturned at it is ABANDONED (this runtime cannot cancel an agent) and dispositioned by kind -- an ADVISORY one degrades to a legible 'skipped -- <agent> unavailable' notice and the item carries on, a MANDATORY one escalates review-agent-timeout carrying the computed tally, so the gate never reads as if it passed. Enforced by racing the fanout against a one-command `sleep` executor, because Date.now() throws in the Workflow runtime and there is no timer primitive (DESIGN NOTE 1); if that timer itself cannot run the bound fails OPEN to the pre-#2003 unbounded await rather than manufacturing an instant false breach. Resolved at build.md/sweep.md/fix.md Step 0 and passed as input.reviewAgentCeilingSecs; the .mjs keeps its own in-file default and FLOORS the value at one CI-poll/gate slice so no operator value can time out healthy work

Observability half of BUILD_REVIEW_AGENT_CEILING_SECS: a §3e review fanout still running after this many seconds emits a log() progress notice naming which reviewers are still outstanding, so a long-but-alive review is visible well before the ceiling gives up on it -- instead of the 41 minutes of silence temperloop#2003 was. A slow review is NOT abandoned and NOT dispositioned. It also sets the timer's FIRST slice, so a review finishing inside this threshold costs exactly one cheap sleep-executor spawn (the micro-agent cost temperloop#942 exists to keep down). 0 disables the notice. Clamped below the ceiling, where it could never fire. Resolved at build.md/sweep.md/fix.md Step 0 and passed as input.reviewAgentSlowSecs

ENV VAR rather than a flag deliberately: a consuming repo vendoring an older quality-gates.sh IGNORES an unknown env var and runs the whole suite (still correct), whereas an unknown flag would exit 2 'usage' and read back to /build's 3e.5 gate as a gate failure (temperloop#1021)

Opt-in per-gate wall-clock breakdown written to $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY, labelled by runner OS (temperloop#968). 0 (the default) emits nothing, so a local run and the merge-path `checks` job are byte-identical to before; the nightly per-OS workflows set 1 to publish the timing table that localises the macOS-vs-ubuntu delta to named gates instead of attributing it to "macOS is slow". Soft per-invocation wall-clock budget for scripts/quality-gates.sh; checked only BETWEEN gates (so no gate is ever killed mid-run) and, when spent with gates remaining, the script prints QUALITY_GATES_RESUME_AT=/QUALITY_GATES_FAILED= and exits 75 (EX_TEMPFAIL, distinct from 0 pass and 1 fail). 0 (the default) disables slicing entirely. /build's 3e.5 gate sets it from BUILD_GATE_SLICE_SECS and loops slices, which is what removes the executor agent's ~10-min Bash cap as a ceiling on total suite runtime (temperloop#1021)

The ENV TWIN of scripts/quality-gates.sh's `--scoped` flag (temperloop#1663): 1 runs only the gates the LOCAL working-tree changes reach, exactly as the flag does; any other value leaves the run full. It exists because /build's 3e.5 acceptance gate reaches this script through a command string whose whole interface is env vars -- a consuming repo vendoring an OLDER quality-gates.sh ignores an unknown env var and runs the whole suite (still correct), whereas an unknown FLAG would exit 2 `usage` and read back to the caller as a gate FAILURE. The flag wins when both are present

File path where a SCOPED run records the changed set it resolved, so a later SLICE of the same suite reuses it instead of re-probing a working tree that may have moved (temperloop#1663). QUALITY_GATES_START_AT is an ORDINAL into the gate list, and a scoped list is re-derived per invocation, so a drifted probe would leave the resume index addressing a DIFFERENT gate -- silently skipping one while the suite still exits 0. Empty (the default) disables pinning, which is correct for a single-shot run with no later slice to drift against. Set by build-level.mjs's 3e.5 gate and removed by it on slice 0, so a re-drive never inherits a previous attempt's pin

The selection fingerprint (<count>:<digest>) the PREVIOUS slice reported on its QUALITY_GATES_SELECTION= line, fed back so this slice can prove it is resuming into the SAME gate list the index was measured in (temperloop#1663). On a mismatch the run does NOT resume the now-meaningless ordinal: it restarts from gate 0 on the FULL set and says so on stderr -- widening, never skipping, the same posture as every other degradation in this selector. Defaults to 1 so an existing invocation is unchanged. Raising it trades run time against the PROVIDER'S RATE LIMIT, not CPU — N concurrent records multiply request rate against one account quota, making a circuit-breaker trip more likely — plus a smaller local-CPU cost, since each leg forks a quality-gates.sh that itself pools up to 4 wide

Age past which a mutation-lock directory that never got a pid file written into it (the mkdir/pid-write window) is treated as debris and stolen (temperloop#1171); a lock whose owner pid is provably dead is stolen immediately regardless of age

How many times create retries a `git worktree add` that lost the .git/config lock to a FOREIGN writer outside worktree.sh’s own lock (temperloop#1171); each failed attempt is rolled back first, so a retry never hits branch-already-exists

Wall-clock bound, in seconds, on the single `git fetch origin <default>` worktree.sh runs to freshen the LOCAL origin/<default> ref every landed-check compares against (temperloop#2030 — a stale comparison point made `remove` record already-merged work as an unlanded refs/parked/* preservation). Enforced through the shared workflows/scripts/lib/portable-timeout.sh shim, so the bound holds on a stock macOS with neither GNU timeout nor gtimeout installed. The bound is FAIL-SAFE by construction: a fetch killed at the bound leaves the local ref as the basis, which can only make work read as LESS landed — i.e. MORE preserved — so a too-short bound degrades toward preserving work, never toward destroying it, and `remove` never depends on the network being up. Every caller records which basis it judged on (basis=refreshed / basis=unrefreshed) on the mint line and on the preservation ref's own reflog.

Repo root the triples extractor resolves the ontology/citation registries and the docs/adr supersession corpus against (registry-maintenance fix, registry-config-lints — the seam's own default is a same-file $VAR indirection, recorded verbatim per this file's own "never pre-resolved" rule; checkout-relative default via git rev-parse --show-toplevel, mirrors CLAIMS_RAW_DIR_DEFAULT's convention)

The harness Workflow tool's hard byte limit on a scriptPath file, restated here ONLY so workflows/scripts/check-workflow-script-size.sh has something to measure against -- it is the HARNESS's constraint, not this repo's, which is exactly why nothing in checks measured it. claude/workflows/build-level.mjs reached 98.4% of it in PR #2114 (the dual-build level barrier, +1084 lines) with no signal of any kind, went over in PR #2125 (the five hand-off fixes, +1453 lines) at 554776 bytes, and the Workflow tool then refused to load it -- stopping /fix, /sweep and /build together, since all three invoke the engine by scriptPath. Both PRs were fully green: the failure is invisible to CI by construction. It is also NOT self-repairing, because the repair would have to be driven by the engine that no longer loads, so it cost a hand repair outside the pipeline. Raise this ONLY if the harness raises its own limit; lowering it is safe and only tightens the guard

Percentage of WORKFLOW_SCRIPT_BYTE_CEILING a claude/workflows/*.mjs file may occupy before check-workflow-script-size.sh FAILS the build. Deliberately well under 100 so the gate fires while there is still room to land the fix, rather than after the engine is already unloadable -- at 100 the guard would only ever confirm an outage that had already happened. The margin also absorbs one ordinary engine PR: temperloop#2114 added 101562 bytes and #2125 added 38642, so a budget that trips near the ceiling would still let a single large change cross in one step. The guard reports headroom in bytes on every PASS, not just a percentage, because a number without its margin does not tell a reader how much room is left
